what_it_does: Quantum computers sometimes need to measure a qubit (the quantum equivalent of a bit) in the middle of a computation and then use that result to decide what to do next — a technique called mid-circuit measurement with classical feedback. The problem is that waiting for the measurement result to finish processing before running the next quantum gate wastes precious time and lets the qubit degrade. ARTERY borrows the idea of 'branch prediction' from ordinary processors — where a CPU guesses which direction an if-statement will go and starts working ahead — and applies it to quantum hardware. It combines two signals: the historical odds that a measurement goes a certain way, and an early look at the shape of the microwave pulse being used to read the qubit (which carries information about the answer even before the full measurement is done). By fusing these two hints, ARTERY lets the quantum controller start the next gate speculatively before the measurement is confirmed, then corrects any mistake cheaply if the guess was wrong. Supporting hardware includes fast links between the control boards (FPGAs, programmable chips that translate software commands into microwave pulses) so multiple qubits can coordinate their feedback quickly.
